chapter: Chano Pozo, Town Hall and Charlie Parker
title: Meeting Charlie Parker at the Palladium rehearsal
summary: Parker listened to "Mango Mangue" twice and played the whole arrangement as if he had known it for years.

story.theme_name: Charlie Parker, Dizzy and the bebop revolution
story.community_name: Charlie Parker: encounters, lore and legacy

blocks.x: When you look back at that now, would you say that he integrated well with the Afro-Cuban music?
Well, he was so talented and he was so sure of what he was doing. He never improvised anything that it was - that he had no sequence. It's not my opinion, the opinion of people more qualified that I.
Do you remember the first time you met him?
Ahh - What do you recall about that meeting?
Oh, he came to the Palladium. We were rehearsing in the afternoon, especially for him. We want him - he wants to listen a few things that we played .....
Was he there with Norman GranZ?

..... and he was there listening to the band. We played on "Mango Mangue", it was an instrumental with no solo or nothing, just an instrumental - playing instrumental, with no solos - and he say: "Play that number, "Mango Mangue". Okay, la re ra uu, we started. We played once, he says: "Play again". He put together his instrument and he played all through the arrangement, like he know that number for twenty years. We played another number, the same thing. That fellow had a photograph, a machine in his brain. Anything that he hear he kept like a sponge like; so it was no problem with him because he was so far advanced. He was so
well equipped in the analysis of chords, that he knew what to do with anything. He was thinking ahead maybe ten, fifteen, twenty bars, with ideas.

He never got by surprise, like a lot of soloists that get by surprise. One idea comes to his mind and then something in the middle interrupts with the next idea; no, he was a sequence - buru buru buru buru - like a machine like.
